title: Renaissance Doctors Came in Four Tiers, and the Best Healer Was Called a Quack
dek: Bone-setters worked the market circuit every week, setting fractures more often than a licensed surgeon saw in a year — and the physicians called them quacks. Title and skill were never the same thing.
why: A medical history interview, medium information density. The value is in the stratification of the medical marketplace, the origins of credential monopoly, and the era when bloodletting, purging and vomiting were enshrined as the three great therapies.
who: Listeners interested in medical history, the origins of professional licensure, and the stratification of medical markets; anyone building or setting policy in health care should hear the part on credential monopoly.
skip: The first two minutes of show promotion and book club announcements can be skipped.

points.h: Eighty to ninety percent of care was provided free by women
points.body: Erin asks who was practicing medicine in this period, and Alanna Skuse's answer is ‘almost everyone’ — but the real base of supply was women: household healers carried roughly 80%, perhaps 90%, of medical care, and most of it was charged very little or nothing at all. The reason they were overlooked by history is concrete — they left too little written material behind. Knowledge passed down the maternal line: mother to daughter, aunt to niece, sometimes mistress to servant, carried in handwritten recipe books. They also wrote to each other swapping ‘I found a good recipe’ and ‘I tried this and it didn't work.’ This formed a medical network with no licenses, no college, that nonetheless covered the vast majority of the population.

points.h: First you check your purse: ten shillings a visit
points.body: The path to care was essentially a price ladder. At the very top was the physician, about 10 shillings a visit, extremely expensive, so only the wealthy called a doctor directly. Those without money worked upward from the bottom: first a local woman, a midwife with extra medical skill, or a nearby gentlewoman with leisure and literacy; failing that, an apothecary, whose medicines started at a penny, like today's pharmacist, except nearly every one sold his own secret remedies and sometimes diagnosed and treated patients himself; failing that, or if a leg was obviously broken, a surgeon, about 3 shillings a visit, who handled everything on the body's surface — lumps, wounds, fractures. Skuse says plainly that how sick you let yourself get before seeking care depended on what it cost: ‘a doctor or dinner.’

points.h: The guild monopoly failed, but the idea of credentials stuck
points.body: Skuse characterizes the motive behind the College of Physicians bluntly as commercial: physicians resented surgeons and barber-surgeons encroaching on their turf and wanted to found a college and then monopolize all medical practice. The college was founded, the monopoly was not obtained — it couldn't even control London, let alone the country. But the long-term consequence matters more than the short-term outcome: this was the first time the idea that ‘healers ought to be credentialed’ took systematic form. Skuse draws the line to today at the end: these institutions, initially weak regulators, evolved into bodies like the British Medical Association and the AMA, and our assumption that doctors share uniform standards and a single opinion starts here.

points.h: Calling rival practitioners quacks was the norm, not the exception
points.body: Asked how fierce competition was among doctors, Skuse says they were ‘horribly rude to each other,’ and finding two who didn't quarrel was rarer than the reverse — because there was only one pie and everyone wanted the biggest slice. So surgeons insulted apothecaries, physicians insulted surgeons, and everyone called everyone else a quack. She gives an example: someone claimed a certain doctor had gone off to exorcise a woman, when in fact she merely had gas. Quack comes from the Dutch quacksalver, meaning someone who peddles ointments by boasting of medical credentials; another word, mountebank, comes from Italian, meaning someone who climbs onto a stage to hawk cures. The key point is that the word's boundary was filthy: a bone-setter would be called a quack by a physician, because he had no credentials and no fixed shop.

points.h: Bone-setters were more skilled than licensed surgeons
points.body: This is the sharpest passage in the whole piece. Skuse asks: if you had a complex fracture, would you go to a licensed surgeon who did a handful a year, or a bone-setter who traveled a different market every week and did nothing but set bones? Bone-setters usually also pulled teeth — teeth rotted badly in that era and there was no remedy but extraction — so they tended to be physically strong, and they brought an equally strong assistant to hold the patient down during the work. Physicians classed these men as quacks, on the grounds of no credentials and no shop. But by actual surgical volume, their skill far exceeded that of their licensed peers. Credentials and competence here are two independent axes.

points.h: Efficacy was not the main source of trust
points.body: Erin asks directly whether efficacy affected trust, and Skuse's answer is: people did not expect to be cured in the first place. They did not expect a life free of pain, nor did they expect a doctor to fix everything wrong with them — but they did judge a doctor for doing the wrong thing. She gives the example of Elizabeth Freke: her husband was gravely ill with a gangrenous leg, she went away for a few days to rest, came back to find him worse, and told the doctor ‘you have murdered my husband.’ So trust was more commercial than clinical: a doctor who gossiped about his patients lost business; a healer who held on could keep a family for life, even across generations — a midwife's daughter delivering the daughter of the woman her mother had delivered. She also mentions Henry Moore bringing a famous physician's prescriptions from the Continent for Lady Anne Conway, when she might have done better with a local doctor.

points.h: Opponents of bloodletting often believed other nonsense too
points.body: Skuse concedes that while the vast majority believed in the humors and bled themselves, there were public dissenters from bloodletting, with George Thompson one of the leading figures of that camp. The problem is that these people often believed other quite absurd things at the same time, which undermined their credibility. On where evidence-based medicine begins, she says it's hard to answer, because in a sense medicine has always had evidence-based medicine: in the 16th century they were already testing antidotes on condemned prisoners, which looks like experiment; what we call the scientific method probably emerged with the Royal Society, and James Lind's scurvy trial in 1746 was the first clinical trial in the modern sense. What actually helped people was mostly gentle remedies — sage and rosemary gargles, ginger and mint for the stomach — along with symptom relief and narrative medicine: a doctor who sat at your bedside for an hour listening to you might have you sleeping better that night.

points.h: Bloodletting, vomiting and purging were named the three great therapies
points.body: Asked about the greatest cost of medical progress, Skuse first gives an institutional answer: surgeons, physicians and apothecaries all crossed each other's boundaries, and it was precisely by crossing boundaries that they learned — at the cost of many patients dying from mercury, arsenic, useless operations and aggressive purging. Because experimentation was not systematic or organized, the toll was far larger than necessary. She also gives a more specific, numerical judgment: the College of Physicians called bloodletting, vomiting and purging the three great therapies, and heaven knows how many people already at death's door were pushed through it by these purging treatments. There was also a cost in quality of life — these therapies were extremely unpleasant.
